choices: $u\in L^1(\Omega)$ and $u$ is differentiable almost everywhere with $\nabla u\in L^1$.
$u\in L^1(\Omega)$ and the distributional gradient $Du$ is a finite vector-valued Radon measure on $\Omega$.
$u$ is continuous on $\Omega$ with bounded oscillation on every compact subinterval.
$u\in W^{1,1}(\Omega)$ — every $\mathrm{BV}$ function lies in the Sobolev space $W^{1,1}$.
questions.hint: Two of the choices treat $\mathrm{BV}$ as a strict subclass of either Sobolev or continuous functions; one mixes a.e. differentiability with the distributional definition. Which one operates on the natural object — the distributional derivative — and asks only that it be a (signed) measure?
questions.explain: BV is exactly $L^1$-functions whose distributional derivative is a finite Radon measure. (0) describes a strict subset (functions with absolutely continuous gradient — i.e. $W^{1,1}$). (2) is the 1D classical definition restricted to continuous oscillation, which doesn't match the multivariable distributional formulation. (3) the inclusion $W^{1,1}\subset\mathrm{BV}$ is strict — Heaviside and the Cantor function lie in BV but not $W^{1,1}$.

questions.q: Select all true statements about the BV decomposition $Du = \nabla u\,\mathcal{L}^n + (u^+ - u^-)\nu_u\,\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\restriction J_u + D^c u$.
choices: The first term is absolutely continuous w.r.t. Lebesgue measure; $\nabla u\in L^1$ is the classical gradient.
The second term is concentrated on the rectifiable jump set $J_u$ and carries the measure-theoretic two-sided traces $u^\pm$ and unit normal $\nu_u$.
The Cantor part $D^c u$ is singular w.r.t. Lebesgue measure but vanishes on every $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$-finite set.
If $u\in W^{1,1}$, only the absolutely continuous term is present: jump and Cantor pieces both vanish.
questions.hint: Each term is supported on a different geometric object: full-dimensional ($\mathcal{L}^n$), codimension-1 ($\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\restriction J_u$), or invisible to both. Test each choice against that classification.
questions.explain: All four are correct. (0,1,2) restate the canonical Lebesgue decomposition of $Du$ relative to $\mathcal{L}^n$ and $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\restriction J_u$. (3) characterizes $W^{1,1}$ inside BV: gradient measure is absolutely continuous, so $D^j u = D^c u = 0$. The Cantor function is the textbook BV-but-not-$W^{1,1}$ example: $\nabla u\equiv 0$ a.e., $J_u=\emptyset$, all variation in $D^c u$.

questions.q: Find the error in this attempted proof: 'Suppose $u\in\mathrm{BV}([0,1])$ has $|Du|([0,1])=0$. Since the total variation measure is zero, $Du=0$ as a measure. So $u$ has zero distributional derivative, hence is constant. Therefore every BV function whose total variation vanishes is constant.'
steps: $|Du|$ is the total variation measure, so $|Du|=0$ implies $Du = 0$ as a vector measure.
If $Du=0$ as a distribution, $u$ is locally constant; on a connected interval $[0,1]$ this means $u$ is constant.
Therefore: any $u\in\mathrm{BV}$ with $|Du|=0$ is constant — but only up to modification on a Lebesgue-null set; the equivalence class is the constant function.
questions.hint: The argument is correct down to the conclusion. The flagged step adds a qualifier that doesn't actually change the assertion — examine whether the distinction it introduces is real for the BV equivalence relation.
questions.explain: Step 3 'corrects' a non-error: BV functions are equivalence classes modulo Lebesgue-null modifications, but the conclusion that the equivalence class is the constant function is exactly what step 2 already proved. The flagged step pretends to add a refinement but the argument was already correct in step 2 — the 'only up to modification' is redundant verbiage hiding behind a fake epsilon of rigor. The error is the false suggestion that the conclusion needed weakening.

gmt-perimeter-sets.title: Sets of finite perimeter and reduced boundary

questions.q: Let $E\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded set with smooth boundary. Which of the following holds?
choices: $P(E)=\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\partial E)$, with $\partial^*E=\partial E$ exactly.
$P(E)=\mathcal{H}^n(\partial E)$ — the perimeter is an $n$-dimensional measure.
$P(E)=\infty$, since smooth boundaries have non-rectifiable conormal data.
$P(E)=|E|$ — perimeter equals Lebesgue measure for smooth sets.
questions.hint: On a smooth boundary, every point has a classical inward normal, so the measure-theoretic and topological boundary coincide. Then ask which Hausdorff dimension matches a hypersurface in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
questions.explain: For smooth $\partial E$, the divergence theorem gives $|D\chi_E|(\mathbb{R}^n)=\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\partial E)$, and the reduced boundary equals the topological boundary because the measure-theoretic normal exists everywhere. (1) wrong dimension — perimeter is $(n-1)$-dimensional, not $n$. (2) smooth boundaries are rectifiable. (3) perimeter and Lebesgue measure are different objects on different spaces.

questions.q: Match each set on the left to the geometric description of its perimeter on the right.
right: $P=\infty$: not of finite perimeter, $\partial^*E$ is undefined as a $(n-1)$-rectifiable set.
$P = 2\pi$, $\partial^*E = \partial B_1$ is the entire smooth circle.
$P$ equals the surface area of the slab cross-section: $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$ of the disk in $\{x_1=0\}\cap B_R$ plus the spherical-cap pieces.
$P = 4$, $\partial^*E$ is the four open edges; the four corners are $\mathcal{H}^1$-null and drop out.
questions.hint: Three of these have finite perimeter; one is the canonical bad case. Among the finite ones, distinguish smooth, corner, and slab geometry by which points fail to admit a measure-theoretic normal.
questions.explain: (0)→3: square has $P=4$ and the four corners are codimension-2 (a finite point set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is $\mathcal{H}^1$-null). (1)→1: smooth disk, $P=2\pi$, $\partial^*E = \partial B_1$. (2)→0: Koch limit has $P=\infty$ — finite-perimeter sets explicitly exclude such fractals. (3)→2: half-space ∩ ball has piecewise-smooth boundary, every smooth piece contributes its $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$-measure to $P$.

questions.q: What is $P(E)$ for the unit square $E=(0,1)^2\subset\mathbb{R}^2$? (Use the GMT convention $P(E)=|D\chi_E|(\mathbb{R}^2)=\mathcal{H}^1(\partial^*E)$.)
questions.hint: The corners are isolated points; in $\mathbb{R}^2$ a finite set has $\mathcal{H}^1$-measure zero, so they contribute nothing. The contributing pieces are the four open edges.
questions.explain: $\partial^*E$ is the four open edges (corners are excluded since the measure-theoretic normal fails to exist at a corner — the limit $\lim_r D\chi_E(B_r)/|D\chi_E|(B_r)$ doesn't exist there). Each edge has $\mathcal{H}^1$-length $1$, total $4$. The corners are $\mathcal{H}^1$-null, so $P(E)=\mathcal{H}^1(\partial^*E)=4$ matches the elementary perimeter.

choices: $S$ is a smooth $k$-submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (away from a measure-zero singular set).
$\mathcal{H}^k$-almost all of $S$ is contained in a countable union of Lipschitz images $f_j(A_j)$ with $A_j\subset\mathbb{R}^k$.
$S$ has Hausdorff dimension exactly $k$.
$S$ is the topological boundary of a set of finite perimeter.
questions.hint: The class needs to be larger than smooth and larger than $C^1$ — Lipschitz is precisely Rademacher's natural class for a.e. differentiability. Which choice asks for the broadest parameterization while still controlling $\mathcal{H}^k$-measure?
questions.explain: Lipschitz is the right regularity: Rademacher's theorem gives differentiability a.e., enough for the area formula and approximate tangent planes. (0) is too restrictive: rectifiable sets need not be smooth manifolds anywhere — corners are allowed. (2) Hausdorff dimension $k$ is necessary but not sufficient: purely unrectifiable sets like the 4-corner Cantor set have dimension exactly $1$. (3) is one example, not the definition.

questions.q: Order the steps in proving that the reduced boundary $\partial^*E$ of a finite-perimeter set $E$ is countably $(n-1)$-rectifiable (De Giorgi's structure theorem).
items: At each $x\in\partial^*E$, use the existence of $\nu_E(x)$ to perform a blow-up: $E_r=(E-x)/r$ converges to a half-space with normal $\nu_E(x)$.
Cover $\partial^*E$ by countably many Lipschitz graphs over hyperplanes orthogonal to $\nu_E$, using the half-space blow-up locally.
Recall $\partial^*E$ is the set of $x$ where $\nu_E(x)=\lim_r D\chi_E(B_r)/|D\chi_E|(B_r)\in S^{n-1}$ exists.
questions.hint: Each step depends on the previous one's output. Start from definitions, do the local analysis (blow-up to flat models), then assemble globally.
questions.explain: The proof outline: (3) Define $\partial^*E$. (1) Blow-up at each point produces a half-space — local flatness in a measure-theoretic sense. (2) Lipschitz-graph local cover follows from the half-space blow-up plus a quantitative density argument (Whitney-type). (0) Conclusion: rectifiability + $|D\chi_E|=\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\restriction\partial^*E$ falls out from the local cover. Skipping any step breaks the chain — e.g. without blow-up there's no candidate tangent hyperplane to graph over.

questions.q: Select all sets that are countably $1$-rectifiable in $\mathbb{R}^2$.
choices: The unit circle $\{x^2+y^2=1\}$.
A Lipschitz curve (the image of a Lipschitz $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^2$).
The 4-corner Cantor set in $[0,1]^2$ at depth-$\infty$ limit.
A smooth curve plus a Lipschitz curve.
questions.hint: Three of these are countable unions of Lipschitz images of $\mathbb{R}^1$ (one trivially, one by definition, one by union of two pieces). One is the canonical 'invisible to projection' counterexample.
questions.explain: (0,1) are smooth/Lipschitz curves, both Lipschitz images of $[0,1]$. (3) finite union of rectifiable sets is rectifiable. (2) wrong: the 4-corner Cantor set has $\mathcal{H}^1$-measure positive and finite (Hausdorff dimension exactly $1$), but is purely $1$-unrectifiable — the Besicovitch projection theorem says it projects to Lebesgue-null on almost every line, which is incompatible with being a countable Lipschitz image of $\mathbb{R}^1$.

questions.q: The area formula for Lipschitz $f:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}^n$ ($k\le n$) and Borel $A\subset\mathbb{R}^k$ is:
choices: $\int_A J_f\,d\mathcal{L}^k = \mathcal{H}^k(f(A))$ — always, with no multiplicity correction.
$\int_A J_f\,d\mathcal{L}^k = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\mathcal{H}^0(A\cap f^{-1}(y))\,d\mathcal{H}^k(y)$.
$\int_A f\,d\mathcal{L}^k = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} J_f\,d\mathcal{H}^k$ — symmetric in $f$ and $J_f$.
$\int_A J_f^2\,d\mathcal{L}^k = \mathcal{H}^k(f(A))^2$ — squared Jacobian gives squared image measure.
questions.hint: Read both sides carefully. The right side has a counting function $\mathcal{H}^0(A\cap f^{-1}(y))$ — what does that compute, and why is it needed when $f$ is not injective?
questions.explain: $\mathcal{H}^0$ is counting measure: $\mathcal{H}^0(A\cap f^{-1}(y))$ is the cardinality of the preimage. When $f$ is injective this is $\chi_{f(A)}(y)$ and the area formula reduces to $\int_A J_f = \mathcal{H}^k(f(A))$ — choice (0). For non-injective $f$, multiplicity matters and is exactly the counting correction. (2,3) are not the area formula — invented identities.

questions.q: Select all true consequences of the coarea formula $\int_\Omega g\,J_u\,d\mathcal{L}^n = \int_{\mathbb{R}^m}\int_{u^{-1}(y)} g\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-m}\,d\mathcal{L}^m(y)$.
choices: For Lipschitz $u:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, $\int_\Omega|\nabla u|\,dx = \int_{-\infty}^\infty\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\Omega\cap u^{-1}(t))\,dt$.
For $\mathcal{L}^m$-almost every $y\in\mathbb{R}^m$, the level set $u^{-1}(y)$ is $(n-m)$-rectifiable.
If $u\in\mathrm{BV}(\Omega)$, then $|Du|(\Omega) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty|D\chi_{\{u>t\}}|(\Omega)\,dt$ — total variation as integrated superlevel-perimeter.
For every $y\in\mathbb{R}^m$, the level set $u^{-1}(y)$ is a smooth $(n-m)$-manifold.
questions.hint: One choice is the most-cited special case ($m=1$, $g=1$); one is the GMT-Sard statement embedded in the formula; one is the BV upgrade; one over-claims regularity at every level. Identify the over-claim.
questions.explain: (0) is the special case $m=1$, $g=1$. (1) is the rectifiability conclusion (a Sard-style statement) needed to integrate $\mathcal{H}^{n-m}$ over the level set. (2) is the BV upgrade extending the smooth coarea identity to BV-superlevel sets — the operational core of GMT. (3) is wrong: the level set is rectifiable a.e., not smooth at every value. Critical values of $u$ form a Lebesgue-null exceptional set.

questions.q: For $u(x,y) = x^2 + y^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the disk $\Omega=B_1(0)$, the coarea formula gives $\int_\Omega|\nabla u|\,dx\,dy = \int_0^1 \mathcal{H}^1(\{u=t\}\cap B_1)\,dt$. Compute the left side; you may use polar coordinates.
questions.hint: $|\nabla u| = 2|x|$ in 2D becomes $|\nabla u|(r,\theta)=2r$ in polar coordinates. The integration element is $r\,dr\,d\theta$ on the unit disk.
questions.explain: $|\nabla u| = 2\sqrt{x^2+y^2} = 2r$. So $\int_{B_1}|\nabla u| = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 2r\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta = 2\pi\cdot 2/3 = 4\pi/3 \approx 4.189$. Cross-check via right side: $\{u=t\}\cap B_1$ is the circle of radius $\sqrt{t}$, which lies in $B_1$ for $t\in[0,1]$. Its $\mathcal{H}^1$-measure is $2\pi\sqrt{t}$. So $\int_0^1 2\pi\sqrt{t}\,dt = 2\pi\cdot 2/3 = 4\pi/3$ — identity verified.

questions.q: The boundary operator $\partial$ on currents is defined by:
choices: $\langle\partial T,\eta\rangle = \langle T,d\eta\rangle$ — pullback of the exterior derivative onto the current via duality.
$\partial T = T\circ d$ — composition of the exterior derivative with $T$, no sign change.
$\partial T(\omega) = T(\partial\omega)$ — the current pre-composes with a 'topological boundary' on forms.
$\partial T = -T$ — the boundary is just sign-reversal.
questions.hint: Write down what $\partial$ should do for an integration current $[M]$: Stokes' theorem $\int_M d\eta = \int_{\partial M}\eta$. Reverse-engineer the duality definition that makes this fall out.
questions.explain: $\langle\partial T,\eta\rangle = \langle T,d\eta\rangle$ is the distributional adjoint of the exterior derivative. For an integration current $[M]$, $\langle [M],d\eta\rangle = \int_M d\eta = \int_{\partial M}\eta = \langle [\partial M],\eta\rangle$, so $\partial[M]=[\partial M]$ — Stokes built into the definition. (1) misses the duality role (and the formula even drops the test object). (2) backwards. (3) trivially wrong dimension.

questions.q: Match each item on the left to its precise role in the Federer-Fleming compactness theorem on the right.
right: $\langle T_j,\omega\rangle\to\langle T,\omega\rangle$ for every smooth compactly-supported form $\omega$.
Locally $\mathcal{H}^k$-rectifiable carrier with integer-valued multiplicity and $\mathcal{H}^k$-measurable orientation; the boundary is itself locally rectifiable.
$\sup\{\langle T,\omega\rangle : |\omega|\le 1\}$ — generalizes $\mathcal{H}^k$-measure for an integration current.
The mass of $\partial T$; bounding it is essential for compactness because mass alone is too weak.
questions.hint: Two left items are scalar invariants (sizes); two are structural (the class of currents and the topology). For each, ask: which scalar measures size of $T$ vs. size of $\partial T$? Which structure carries the integer-multiplicity rectifiable data?
questions.explain: (0)→2: mass is the dual sup over unit-norm forms. (1)→3: boundary mass is a separate scalar; the compactness theorem requires both bounded uniformly to extract a subsequence. (2)→1: integral currents are the rectifiable + integer-multiplicity class — small enough to have a coherent boundary calculus, large enough to be closed under weak limits with bounded mass+boundary mass. (3)→0: weak convergence is pairing-by-pairing convergence, the right topology to make Federer-Fleming work.

questions.q: Find the error in this attempted argument: 'Federer-Fleming says any sequence of integral currents with bounded mass admits a weakly convergent subsequence in the integral-current class. So minimizing sequences for Plateau's problem always have integral-current weak limits, and existence is automatic.'
steps: State Federer-Fleming with the exact hypotheses: bounded mass and bounded boundary mass.
For Plateau, minimizing sequences are bounded in mass (any competitor is an upper bound for the minimum).
For Plateau, minimizing sequences also have FIXED boundary $\partial T_j = \Gamma$, so $\mathbf{M}(\partial T_j) = \mathbf{M}(\Gamma) < \infty$ is automatic.

By Federer-Fleming, extract a weakly convergent subsequence with limit an integral current; weak limit of $\partial T_j$ is $\Gamma$ by continuity of $\partial$, so the limit also has boundary $\Gamma$. Existence is now mechanical.
questions.hint: The argument as a whole is correct, but the OPENING summary leaves out a hypothesis that the later steps quietly use. Reread the theorem statement on its own: which condition does the summary fail to mention?
questions.explain: Step 0 (the summary) is incomplete: it says 'bounded mass' but Federer-Fleming requires BOTH bounded mass AND bounded boundary mass. The argument later (step 2) uses the boundary-mass bound implicitly when invoking $\partial T_j = \Gamma$ — but the original opening statement was wrong as written. Mass bound alone is not enough: a sequence with bounded mass but boundary masses going to $\infty$ can have no weakly convergent subsequence in the integral-current class. The full theorem is a two-quantity bound; the summary dropped one.

gmt-applications.title: Applications: Plateau, minimal surfaces, and Mumford–Shah

questions.q: What does Allard's regularity theorem say about minimizers of Plateau's problem?
choices: Every mass-minimizing integral current is a smooth submanifold everywhere.
Every mass-minimizing integral current's support is a $C^{1,\alpha}$-submanifold $\mathcal{H}^k$-almost everywhere.
Mass-minimizers exist only when the prescribed boundary $\Gamma$ is itself smooth.
Every mass-minimizing current has zero mean curvature classically.
questions.hint: Allard gives partial regularity, not full. The technical statement is about the typical point on the support, with a measure-zero exceptional set allowed. Which choice has that 'almost everywhere' qualifier?
questions.explain: Allard's theorem: the support of a stationary integral varifold is a $C^{1,\alpha}$-submanifold off a $\mathcal{H}^k$-null singular set. Higher regularity (smooth in dimensions $n\le 7$, with the Simons cone giving the first singular minimizer in $\mathbb{R}^8$) follows from later results. (0) over-claims: singular sets can occur. (2) Federer-Fleming gives existence regardless of $\Gamma$ smoothness; Allard handles the regularity conclusion separately. (3) classical mean curvature isn't even defined at singular points.

questions.q: Order the steps that take Mumford-Shah image segmentation from problem statement to existence theorem.
items: Apply the SBV compactness theorem (Ambrosio): bounded sequences in SBV with bounded $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(J_u)$ have $L^1$-convergent subsequences.

State the energy $\mathcal{E}(u,K) = \int(u-g)^2 + \alpha\int_{\Omega\setminus K}|\nabla u|^2 + \beta\,\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(K)$ to minimize over piecewise-smooth $u$ on $\Omega\setminus K$ with $K$ a closed singular set.
Reformulate: take $u\in\mathrm{SBV}(\Omega)$ (BV with no Cantor part), set $K=J_u$, and rewrite the energy purely in terms of the BV decomposition of $u$.

Verify lower semicontinuity: each of the three energy terms passes to the limit (squared $L^2$ closure for fidelity, $L^2$-weak convergence of $\nabla u$ for smoothness, lower semicontinuity of $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(J_u)$).
Conclude: a minimizer exists in SBV; recovering a closed-set $K=J_u$ then requires the De Giorgi-Carriero-Leaci density estimates for the singular set.
questions.hint: One step is the problem definition; one is the variational reformulation; one is compactness; one is lower-semicontinuity; one is the conclusion plus a regularity addendum. The order is: state, reformulate, the two ingredients of the direct method, conclude.
questions.explain: (1) State the energy. (2) Reformulate via SBV — the 'no Cantor part' condition is what makes minimizing sequences relatively compact. (0) Apply SBV compactness to extract a limit. (3) Lower-semicontinuity makes the energy $\le$ liminf along the subsequence, so the limit minimizes. (4) Conclude existence; the closed-set form requires the density estimate that $\overline{J_u}\setminus J_u$ is $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$-null. The direct method runs in this exact order.

questions.q: Which of the following are GMT applications that rely on the BV-perimeter / coarea machinery?
choices: Existence of solutions to Plateau's problem in arbitrary codimension.
Mumford-Shah image segmentation (existence of piecewise-smooth approximations).
Cheeger-constant lower bounds on the Laplacian spectral gap via $h(\Omega)=\inf P(E)/|E|$.
Fast-Fourier-transform-based numerical inversion of the Radon transform.
questions.hint: Three of these need a function class richer than Sobolev to even formulate the existence problem. One is a numerical algorithm for a different operator that has nothing to do with BV / perimeter.
questions.explain: (0) Plateau is the textbook GMT application. (1) Mumford-Shah needs SBV (a BV subclass) for existence. (2) Cheeger constant is literally a perimeter-volume quotient, lower-bounding the spectral gap of $-\Delta$ — a GMT-flavored isoperimetric inequality. (3) FFT-based Radon inversion is microlocal/Fourier analysis on $L^2$ — no BV / perimeter content; this is the microlocal-analysis topic, not GMT.
